pages.text: The motion was “This house believes that students should be allowed to use phones in school.” Felicia Owusu’s palms were wet. The debate club had lost a speaker, and Wilfred, the captain, had asked her to fill in. “I cannot speak in front of people,” she whispered. “You do not have to be loud,” said Wilfred. “You just have to be clear.”

pages.text: Mr Baidoo, the debate master, explained how an argument works. “Make a claim. Give a reason. Give evidence. Explain how the evidence supports the claim.” He wrote on the board: Claim, Reason, Evidence, Link. “An opinion is not an argument,” he said. “‘I like phones’ is an opinion. ‘Phones help students look up answers, because they hold dictionaries and encyclopedias’ is the start of an argument.”

pages.text: Felicia’s team was assigned the side against phones. She did not even like that side. “That is the point,” said Mr Baidoo. “A good debater can argue either side, because they understand both.” Felicia went to the library. She found a report about students’ attention and noted its title and year. She wrote three points on her cards and practised at home in front of a mirror.

pages.text: On the day of the debate, the hall was full. The other side’s first speaker spoke well, and Felicia’s knees shook. Then it was her turn. She stood at the lectern and took a breath. “Mr Chairman, honourable judges, ladies and gentlemen,” she began. Her voice trembled, then steadied. “We do not say phones are bad. We say that a classroom needs focus. Here are three reasons.”

pages.text: In the rebuttal round, the other team’s speaker said, “Those who oppose phones live in the past!” Wilfred leaned over and whispered, “Do not attack the person. Answer the point.” Felicia stood up. “My opponent says we live in the past,” she said calmly. “That is not an argument. The question is whether phones help students learn in class. Here is the evidence that they sometimes do not.”

pages.text: The judges counted the points. “The winner,” announced Mr Baidoo, “is the proposition.” Felicia’s team had lost by two points. Felicia’s heart sank, and then she saw Mr Baidoo smiling. “Your speech was the best argued in the hall,” he said. “Winning matters, but learning to disagree respectfully matters more.” Felicia smiled. “I would do it again,” she said, and she meant it.

pages.text: That evening, Felicia wrote to her friend Yvonne, putting her address and the date at the top. “House 4, Church Street, Winneba. 9th May, 2027. Dear Yvonne, I hope you are well. Today I took part in my first school debate, and I was extremely nervous. Our team did not win, but I spoke clearly and learned how to build an argument. I would like to invite you to watch the next one. Please reply soon. Your friend, Felicia.”

pages.text: Exam-safe tip: Felicia used the same shape as a good argument in her letter, with a clear point, a reason and a conclusion. She also kept a polite, positive tone, even about losing. Notice that she wrote “extremely nervous” and not “super nervous lol”. Strong words and full sentences make a letter persuasive. The end.
